draft.title: Direct and indirect characterisation
card: the writer tells the reader what a character is like. Example: "Leo was a generous boy."
the writer shows what a character is like and lets the reader work it out. Example: Leo hands half his lunch to a classmate who forgot theirs.
Indirect characterisation can use what a character says, does and thinks, and how other characters react to them.
Direct characterisation is quick and clear. Indirect characterisation asks the reader to infer, so it can feel more lifelike.
draft.remember: Direct tells you the trait. Indirect shows you clues so you can work it out.

a.q: Which sentence is an example of direct characterisation?
opts: Priya was a shy and nervous girl
Priya stared at her shoes and whispered her name
Priya's classmates leaned in to hear her speak
Priya thought, "Please don't pick me"
a.why: The first sentence states outright what Priya is like. The others show her shyness through what she does, how others react and what she thinks, so the reader has to infer it.
a.clue: Which one simply tells you the trait?

b.q: In a story, Mr Okafor sighs, checks his watch and snaps at a student who asks a question. Which statement is correct?
opts: This is indirect characterisation of an impatient teacher
This is direct characterisation of an impatient teacher
This is direct characterisation because it names a person
This is indirect because it uses only what he says
This is indirect characterisation because it uses dialogue only
b.why: The writer never states that he is impatient. His actions and words show it, so the reader infers it. The last option is tempting, but indirect characterisation also uses actions, not only dialogue.
b.clue: Does the writer ever name the trait?
